So, Saul is dead but his family remains. Among them is General Abner. After Saul’s death, Abner feels slighted by the family and decides to support David instead. David is pleased. Amnner comes with 20 men to David at Hebr. David hosts a feast for Amnner and his men. Amnner proposes making David king over all of Israel in exchange for his service as general.

David dismisses Abner and leaves peacefully. Job, who is David's general, returns from a raid bringing much spoil with him. However, Abner is not present at Hebron because he has been dismissed by David. When Job learns that Abner was dismissed, he becomes angry, especially since Abner killed one of his brothers. Job questions why David dismissed Abner, suspecting foul play. According to Job, Abner came to deceive David and learn about his movements.

Job leaves David's presence and sends messengers after Abner, bringing him back from the Christian mission of Sarah without David’s knowledge. Job then kills Abner. The story reveals that Job likely rebelled with David’s tacit permission because David is more afraid of a general with an army like Job. This fear leads to David potentially ordering Job to eliminate Abner as a potential threat.

The story, though a lie, provides clues for reconstructing the truth. Unlike other religious texts which are sayings or truisms, this narrative allows us to reimagine and understand the dynamics of loyalty and betrayal among leaders like David and his generals. The spring campaign sees David send Job with officers and all Israel. Despite Job’s past disobedience and killing of Abner, he is never punished, suggesting continued support from David.

Late one afternoon, David sees Bathsheba bathing from the roof of his house and sends someone to inquire about her.
